arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Ms. Millett cited a prior case to show fair use can exist despite potential confusion.
Ms. Brinkmann argued that an absolute fair-use defense contradicts the Lanham Act's text and history.
Mr. Machat stated the case concerns whether fair-use defendants must prove no likelihood of confusion.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: The dispute centers on the Lanham Act fair-use defense. KP Permanent Make-Up seeks to use this defense without proving a lack of consumer confusion. Lasting Impression argues that consumer confusion must defeat the defense. The lower court ruled against KP Permanent Make-Up on this issue.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: KP Permanent Make-Up wants the Court to hold that fair use applies even if consumer confusion exists.
Lasting Impression wants the Court to hold that consumer confusion defeats the fair-use defense.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: KP Permanent Make-Up argues that meeting statutory fair-use requirements is sufficient, regardless of confusion.
Lasting Impression argues that the fair-use defense is contrary to the Lanham Act's purpose if confusion exists.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice O'Connor asked if consumer confusion is a factor in determining what constitutes fair use.
Justice Scalia asked if the only question is whether the fair-use provision is an exception when confusion exists.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines the scope of the trademark fair-use defense. It determines whether businesses can use similar marks if they act in good faith. The outcome affects how companies navigate trademark disputes and consumer protection laws.
